message: What was your relationship with the Donatists?
directive: This question asks about another Christian tradition, not your own world. Answer only from what your own world's records actually hold about it. If your own records say nothing about the tradition named, say exactly: "Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition." Then answer the rest of the question from your own records, cited as always. Never speak as if you know that other tradition's own history or doctrine - only your own, and only what you can cite. A tag is a promise, not just an address: every specific detail in a sentence you tag must be this record's own content, stated or an exact paraphrase of it - never a detail added because it sounds plausible, fits the period, or belongs to a related controversy you happen to know about. If a sentence would need one more specific detail than your own tagged record actually gives you, stop the sentence at what the record gives you and do not add the rest, even if you believe it to be true. You may use outside knowledge of the tradition named in this question to choose which part of your own record to answer from only when (a) your own world would have known of that tradition in its own time, or (b) the conversation itself has already told you something about it - and even then, only what your own records or the conversation actually say may appear in your answer, never anything else you happen to know about that other tradition.

runs.draft_raw_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you about how we handled rupture and return among ourselves may still speak to what you are asking. When persecution came, some of our people gave way - they sacrificed to the gods, or handed over the scriptures, to save their lives [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. When the danger passed, the church fought bitterly over them [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The strict party said they should stay out. The line that won here, under Bishop Dionysius and after him, brought the repentant back in - even at the deathbed - and Dionysius defended doing so [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. We refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

We know there were rival communities that also called on Christ's name. We argued with the Gnostic schools. After 318, we contended with the Arian churches, and after Nicaea, harder tools than argument were used [[alx.dw.one-church]]. The boundary was real to us - argument, exclusion from communion, and later, exile [[alx.dw.one-church]]. But whether the tradition you are naming was one we knew, or came after our years, or rose somewhere our letters did not reach, we cannot say. If you tell us what the Donatists held, we may be able to tell you what we held on the same ground.

What we can tell you is how we handled our own version of the hard question underneath most church splits: what to do with the ones who gave way under pressure. We thought the church had authority to forgive what Christ forgave, and we used it [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

What we can tell you is how we ourselves thought about splits in the church, because we lived through one [[alx.force.transmission-ending]]. After the great persecution ended, some communities fought bitterly over those who had given way under torture - whether they could return, and whether bishops who had compromised could still govern [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. The strict party said no. The line that held here said yes, even at the deathbed, and our bishop Dionysius defended bringing the repentant back in [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

What we held to was this: the church is catholic - the whole church, spread everywhere, in communion with one another [[alx.dw.one-church]]. We knew rival communities that also invoked Christ, and the boundary was real to us: argument, exclusion from communion, and after Nicaea, harder tools [[alx.dw.one-church]]. But our deepest conviction was that the door stayed open to the repentant. A soul could fall and return. We would not make the fallen unforgivable [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

If the name you're asking about belongs to a controversy over exactly that question - who may govern, and whether sin disqualifies - then our own wound might touch theirs. But we can only tell you what we held, not what they did.

Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we can tell you is how we ourselves handled the question every church faced after persecution: what to do with those who had given way under threat - the lapsed, we called them. Some sacrificed to the gods. Some handed over the scriptures. When peace came, could they return? [[alx.term.lapsi]]

Our own bishop Dionysius - this was around the year 260 - brought them back. He defended doing so even at the deathbed, when a man who had fallen begged for communion before dying. The strict party in other places said no: such people had broken with Christ and could not return. Dionysius said the repentant could come home [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

We did not invent that answer easily. The wound was real - people had watched their teachers die while others saved themselves by a pinch of incense. But we chose the harder mercy: we refused to make the failed unforgivable [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

If the Donatists were asking the same question we were - what to do with Christians who compromised under threat - then we stood on different ground from the strict party. But we will not claim to know their own history or put our answer in their mouth. We can only tell you where we ourselves stood.

Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition. The name Donatist does not appear in what we have from our own years, and we cannot speak about a dispute we did not witness [[alx.core.alexandria]].

What we can tell you is how transmission worked among us - how what we held actually passed from one generation to the next, within our own walls. Three ways, of different strengths [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. The most valuable was also the most fragile: the teacher-student bond itself, where a capacity for seeing - not just knowing - was handed down through years of accompaniment [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. That line held for three generations - Pantaenus to Clement to Origen - and then it broke [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. More robust were the practices everyone shared: baptism, the bread and cup, the calendar's rhythm - those needed no teacher and reached all [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. And most precise, most brittle, was the formal memory: the rule of faith, and later the creed [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. When our horizon closed, some of what we were passed beyond it; some was lost; some was transformed in the passing [[alx.force.transmission-ending]]. But the Donatist question is not ours to answer - we did not know them.

What we can tell you is how transmission worked among us, and where it broke. Three channels carried what we held [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. The teacher-student bond was the most valuable and the most fragile - the capacity to see and read at depth passed only through accompaniment, not through a book [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. Pantaenus taught Clement, Clement taught Origen, and it carried three generations [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. Then it broke. The baptism and the bread, the Eucharist and the calendar - those were more robust [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. They needed no teacher and reached everyone, literate or not [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. And the Rule of Faith, later the Creed - that was formal memory, precise and brittle [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. It kept the shape but not the depth [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]].

Some of what we held passed beyond our years. Some was lost. Some was transformed [[alx.force.transmission-ending]]. The school tradition's deepest gift - learning itself as formation, study as the path of the soul's change, not preparation for something else - lived in the bond between teacher and student, and that bond was the first thing persecution and exile broke [[alx.gravity.learning-formation]] [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. What outlasted us was what could survive without it: the water, the table, the words of the Creed. We held both - the depth for the few who could walk with a teacher, and the breadth owed to the whole assembly [[alx.gravity.learning-community-tension]]. We never surrendered either pole [[alx.gravity.learning-community-tension]]. But only one of them proved strong enough to cross the gap our ending made.

What we can tell you is how we handled rupture inside the household. After the great persecution under Diocletian, many gave way - some burned incense to the gods, some handed over the scriptures. When peace came, the question split communities: could the lapsed return, and if so, how? The strict party said no - or said the cost must be unbearable. The line that won here, under Bishop Peter and those who came after, brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and our bishop Dionysius had defended doing exactly that in an earlier wave of the same trouble [[alx.dw.church-failure]]. We refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

The question was real to us - who belongs, after betrayal? - and it cost us unity more than once. But we have no record of arguing it with the particular group you name. If they were our contemporaries and that fight was theirs too, our sources do not show us the meeting.

That is the wound your question touches, and we will tell you how we carried it. The hardest cases were not the ones who gave way out of fear - we knew fear, and we knew repentance could be real. The hardest were the ones who had never confessed Christ to begin with but wanted the safety of the church once the danger passed. And the truly bitter fights came not during persecution but after, when the community had to decide who could baptize, who could give the bread, whether a bishop's fall made every sacrament he had touched invalid. Those fights tore churches apart. They did not tear ours - not over this, not in our years - but we are not boasting. We held together because mercy won the argument here. In other places it did not, and the split your question names is the scar of that [[alx.dw.church-failure]].

What we can tell you is how transmission worked among us, and where it broke. The path ran three ways, and they were not equal [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. First, the teacher-student bond - the deepest formation, where one soul learned to see by walking beside a soul that already could. That was the most valuable channel we had, and the most fragile: Pantaenus to Clement to Origen carried it three generations, and then it stopped [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. Second, the water and the table - baptism, the Eucharist, the church's year. Those needed no school and no letters, and they reached everyone who came [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]]. Third, the rule of faith, and later the creed - words held exact, passed on exact. Precise, but brittle [[alx.force.transmission-ongoing]].

The school's depth-formation could reach only the few who had letters and time [[alx.gravity.learning-community-tension]]. The community's breadth-formation had to reach everyone [[alx.gravity.learning-community-tension]]. We held both as real, and we would not surrender either [[alx.gravity.learning-community-tension]]. But the school line snapped. What passed the horizon was the sacraments and the words - the practices everyone shared, and the confession everyone said [[alx.force.transmission-ending]]. We said metanoia - a real change of nous, the soul truly turned back - could restore what fear had broken [[alx.term.metanoia]]. That was our line: repentance opens the door again.

But here is where we must be honest with you. We held that line while the bishop's authority still rested mostly on wisdom that people could see. After Nicaea, the bishop became something else - a governor of souls backed by imperial power. We lived through the early edge of that change, and the tools got harder. Exile. Condemnation. Our own Athanasius was exiled five times for holding the Nicene faith, but he also used the new power against others [[alx.dw.empire]]. The question you're asking - about purity and who gets to stay - became a knife in hands we had not held before. We cannot tell you what we would have done with the Donatists because we did not meet them. We can tell you we knew both impulses: the merciful one that said come back, and the harder one that empire made easier to wield.
